Given the formulation, maladaptive strategies should connect plausibly back to the listed triggers; this item is poorly matched.

vignette:
Ravi, a 50-year-old animator of South Asian descent, sought therapy after years of escalating distress following his son Rohan’s life-threatening illness five years prior. Rohan, then a toddler, had been struck by a sudden, severe autoimmune condition that required an extended stay in the pediatric intensive care unit. Ravi recounted those weeks as a blur of fear and helplessness, sleeping on a cot beside Rohan’s bed, the constant beeping of machines and the sterile, antiseptic smell of the hospital becoming the backdrop to his waking nightmares. He remembered watching the medical teams perform procedure after procedure, his heart seizing with each new intervention, convinced he was witnessing his child slip away. Though Rohan made a full recovery, those memories remained raw, shaping Ravi’s every waking moment.

Now, even the slightest hint of antiseptic cleaner in a public restroom or the distinct odor of a doctor’s office could plunge Ravi into a profound state of anxiety. These olfactory triggers, along with the thought of any medical procedure, for himself or his family, would immediately activate a torrent of distressing thoughts. He found himself consumed by a simmering rage, constantly ruminating on how to get even with the abstract "assailant" that had threatened his son's life, whether it was the illness itself, the perceived slowness of initial diagnosis, or the sheer injustice of it all. This rumination often morphed into a relentless mental rehearsal of worst-case scenarios, where he would meticulously play out every terrifying detail of Rohan falling ill again, or even worse, dying, believing that by anticipating the worst, he could somehow prepare himself or prevent it from happening. This constant mental activity, far from making him feel prepared, only heightened his internal alarm, making him feel perpetually on edge. This incessant mental rehearsal of catastrophic medical scenarios made any actual thought or mention of a medical procedure for himself or his family an even more immediate and potent trigger, as his mind was already primed with vivid, terrifying images.

The relentless cycle of worst-case rehearsal and rumination had a profound impact on Ravi’s daily life. He became hyper-vigilant, constantly scanning his environment and his family for any sign of illness or danger. This meant that the thought of sleeping alone, or even in an unfamiliar place like a hotel room during a work trip, became unbearable. He would feel a surge of panic, convinced that if he wasn't physically present, something catastrophic would befall his family, particularly Rohan. The anxiety from this trigger would then feed back into his maladaptive strategies, reinforcing his need to mentally rehearse every possible negative outcome, from his son having a fever to a sudden accident. He found himself increasingly asking his wife, Priya, for reassurance that everything was okay, that he was okay, that Rohan was truly safe. Priya, though patient, was growing weary of the constant need for validation.

At work, the vibrant, imaginative world of animation that Ravi once loved became a struggle. His focus was fractured, his creativity stifled by the intrusive thoughts. He would often spend hours mentally rehearsing scenarios instead of animating, leading to missed deadlines and increased stress. The escalating anxiety and the exhausting mental gymnastics had taken a toll on his sleep, leaving him perpetually fatigued and irritable. He knew he couldn't continue living this way, constantly battling an invisible enemy and trapped in a loop of fear and preparedness that offered no real peace. He came to therapy hoping to find a way out of the relentless cycle, exhausted by the constant vigilance and the fear that, despite all his efforts, the worst might still happen.
